subsections.subsection_title: WHAT WOULD YOU DO IF THE PATIENT IS UNSTABLE?

blocks.text: “I would immediately recognise this as a major postpartum haemorrhage with haemodynamic compromise. I would call for senior obstetric and anaesthetic assistance and alert the theatre and blood bank teams. I would perform an ABCDE assessment, insert two large-bore IV cannulas, take blood for FBC, group and crossmatch, coagulation studies, fibrinogen, U&E and blood gas, and begin appropriate resuscitation and blood products according to the major haemorrhage protocol. I would quantify ongoing blood loss, insert a urinary catheter and continuously monitor the patient. Simultaneously, I would assess the uterus and placenta and examine for genital tract trauma, working systematically through the four Ts: tone, tissue, trauma and thrombin. I would give appropriate uterotonics and early tranexamic acid, and if bleeding persisted I would escalate to balloon tamponade and surgical management, including hysterectomy if necessary.”
That is an excellent high-level OSCE answer.
Bleeding + firm uterus = Trauma until proven otherwise.

Ensure blood availability when high risk.

content_groups.group_title: Q9. What are the indications for balloon tamponade?

blocks.text: Ongoing PPH, particularly suspected uterine atony, when pharmacological treatment and basic measures have failed and appropriate causes have been addressed/excluded.

content_groups.group_title: Q10. When would you perform hysterectomy?

blocks.text: When haemorrhage is life-threatening and cannot be controlled by less invasive measures, or when the underlying pathology makes hysterectomy necessary, such as severe placenta accreta spectrum.

content_groups.group_title: Q11. What is the danger of placenta accreta?

blocks.text: Attempted manual removal may cause catastrophic haemorrhage because the placenta is abnormally adherent to the myometrium.

content_groups.group_title: Q12. What blood products might be required?

blocks.text: Red cells, plasma and platelets, with fibrinogen replacement where indicated, guided by clinical condition, laboratory/viscoelastic results and the local major haemorrhage protocol.

“This is a major obstetric haemorrhage. I would call for senior obstetric and anaesthetic assistance, alert the theatre and blood bank teams, and begin ABCDE resuscitation immediately. I would insert two large-bore IV cannulas, take blood for FBC, group and crossmatch, coagulation studies, fibrinogen and other relevant investigations, commence appropriate resuscitation and blood products, quantify blood loss, insert a urinary catheter and continuously monitor her. Simultaneously, I would identify the cause using the four Ts: tone, tissue, trauma and thrombin. I would massage a boggy uterus, administer appropriate uterotonics and early tranexamic acid, assess the placenta and examine for genital tract trauma. If bleeding continued, I would escalate to balloon tamponade and surgical or interventional management, including hysterectomy if required to save the patient's life.”
That is the core PPH OSCE answer you should be able to deliver confidently under pressure.
